facts.claim: Margaret Glaspy wrote all the songs on Emotions and Math, including the title track, and produced the record herself.
The title song 'Emotions and Math' is credited as written and produced by Margaret Glaspy.
Credits list Chris Morrissey on bass, Tim Kuhl on drums and percussion, Tyler Chester on keyboards, and Glaspy on guitar and vocals. Julian Lage is credited as production manager.
Chris Allen engineered the album, Shawn Everett mixed it, and Emily Lazar mastered it at The Lodge. It was recorded at Sear Sound in New York City.
After the ATO deal was secured, Glaspy re-recorded the entire album at Sear Sound with Morrissey, Kuhl and Chester.

Glaspy said the phrase 'Emotions and Math' was wrapped into a song she was working on and became the album title. She said it fit because she was making something emotive that was also process-driven and analytical.
Glaspy had planned to release the album herself via Bandcamp, but ATO Records picked up her music and released the LP. This followed six years in New York spent babysitting and playing shows.
NPR critic Ken Tucker said the album blends complexity with 'deceptive directness.' He noted that the title song has an angry bite in the vocal that is echoed by a barbed guitar hook.
Emotions and Math was Glaspy's first full-length album. It followed two self-released EPs, Homeschool and If & When, and her studies at Berklee College of Music.

Glaspy toured behind Emotions and Math for about three years. Her 2020 follow-up Devotion came after a hiatus, and her third album Echo the Diamond (2023) was co-produced with her partner, guitarist Julian Lage.

research.lineage: Glaspy sits in the indie rock and folk singer-songwriter tradition, pairing a raw, bluesy guitar-driven rock edge with pop song structures.

draft:
There's a bath in this song, and it isn't relaxing. On **Emotions and Math**, Margaret Glaspy's narrator spends the nights her partner is away awake until 4 a.m. and the mornings hitting snooze, and she sums up the state in one cold, exact image: "Shiverin' in an ice cold bath / Of emotions and math." The longing is there. So is the counting of days, the tally kept because tallying feels like control when nothing else does. Glaspy said the phrase fit the whole record because she was making something emotive that was also process-driven and analytical. Here that tension stops being a working method and becomes the narrator's problem.

What makes the song sting is that she won't let herself off the hook. Things are fine together, she sings, and it's a shame, and she's the one to blame. Then comes the line that carries the most weight: "I'm a woman actin' like a kid." It's a confession that is also a scolding. She pictures herself stuck out on a tree limb, a skinny mess left breathless from listing everything she's going to do. Big promises, little follow-through, and she knows it. The sharpest turn is the pride she lets slip. She used to be a rolling stone, out on her own, borrowing an old rock-and-blues picture of the drifter, and now that someone's here she lives in fear of them leaving. Independence and dependence sit in the same verse, and neither one wins.

The band plays it with almost no fuss. A clean electric guitar picks out arpeggiated chords, the bass walks underneath, and the drums keep a plain kick, snare and hi-hat pattern at a moderate, easy pace. The room sounds open and natural, and each instrument has its own space. Glaspy's voice is clear with a little breath in it, and she sings unadorned and alone. NPR's Ken Tucker heard an angry bite in that vocal, echoed by a barbed guitar hook. That fits a record he described as having a "deceptive directness": the surface stays calm while the words cut.

Glaspy wrote and produced the song herself. It was her first full-length album, which ATO picked up after six years of babysitting and playing shows in New York and a plan to put it out on Bandcamp. She re-recorded it at Sear Sound with Chris Morrissey on bass and Tim Kuhl on drums. That history of waiting and stubbornly doing it yourself suits a song about someone who has proved she can stand alone and now hates how badly she wants company.

It sticks because it admits something most love songs dress up: missing someone can make you feel small, and you can still keep counting the days.
